status: John approved both photographs for A stake for tall brassicas on 19 November 2026.

generator.revision_prompt:
Perform a precise, limited photographic edit of the provided current two-panel photographic sequence. One 1536×1024 landscape diptych, with the unmarked vertical seam at x=768, equal portrait halves. The whole exact allotment composition is protected: replicate the same mature Brussels sprout plant with the same irregular leaf/canopy silhouette and small buds, background, soil, ground entry of plant and stake, the same modest weathered squared timber stake, framing, light and two hands. Use input 1 as the exact photo to edit. Input 2 is actual close footage of used rope and a staked Brussels sprout in the same allotment, for authentic worn rope texture, the stem and the surroundings only. Do not reproduce its rope routing. Use only these two local changes; preserve manual registration of both pictures.

LEFT: swap only the wooden mallet for a real, small BRITISH BUILDER'S LUMP HAMMER (club hammer). It has a squat, chunky double-faced forged dark steel head, square flat striking faces with worn bevelled edges, dull charcoal metal with a slight rub to the bevel and a few old marks. Keep the same ordinary used short wooden handle gripped in the right-hand position. The head is a solid steel block high enough to be recognisable but restrained, roughly two stake widths across. The flat steel lower striking face is parallel to and directly above the flat top of the timber stake, with a hair of visible air at the instant before the blow. The support hand stays well below the head at the same location. No rubber or wooden head, no claw, no long handle, no changes to the forearms, stem or background. No tie added to this stage.

RIGHT: remove all of the previous clean blue tie completely from its low position. The new single tie moves genuinely HIGH, 25–35 pixels below the top of the existing post on the 1536×1024 canvas. The top end of the post is at y≈516, so centre the rope at about y≈548, within about one post-width from the very top. Keep the post top and length where they are. Use a short length of plainly REUSED thin three-strand rope, around 7 mm thick relative to the timber, faded dusty blue-grey with traces of old pale fibres, softly worn surface and two short worn cut ends. Natural muted colour yet enough contrast against green. Avoid cosmetic perfectly even weave, fresh cloth tape, bulk, long tails, gratuitous grime or exaggerated fraying.

Make a single functional loose figure-of-eight. At that high height, one end passes BEHIND and all the way around the real green main stem and returns across its front. The rope must read as a physically continuous loop completely encircling the main stalk itself, not around a leaf stalk or a sprout. In particular the near arc visibly rests against the real front-left stem surface with a small contact shadow. Keep only a little ease on the far side for growth; absolutely no roving gap or floating loop, no rope clipping through plant tissue. If a petiole or sprout occludes the contact, adjust the edge of one adjacent leaf behind the tie just enough to see a clean section of stalk between two nodes. Do not remove or strip the general foliage. The second loop fits around the post, and the two short diagonals CROSS ONCE in the gap between the real stalk and the timber, demonstrably one over the other. Two short ends tied off near the outer side of the stake. Make sure the rope can be traced continuously. Include ONE small weathered U-SHAPED GALVANISED METAL STAPLE visibly driven into the timber face near the top of the post at the height of this rope loop. The arched metal bridge visibly GOES OVER and retains a single rope run against the wood so it cannot slide downward; both legs vanish into the timber, one just above and one just below the secured rope. The metal is grey, compact and actually overlaps the rope, not an isolated mark, screw or shiny buckle. Show slight shading where the rope touches stem and where the staple seats against wood. The finished photographic detail should be convincing and easy to follow.

Keep the view matched and protect every other area including photo height, the tops of the images and the soil at the bottom. No border, caption, insets, text, arrows or new props. Return the full matched photographic pair.
generator.fastener_contact_correction:
Local precision photographic correction. Input 1 is the exact full 1536×1024 two-panel photograph. Return the complete diptych at identical scale, framing, borderless centre seam and camera. Preserve the entire LEFT picture including the correct dark steel builder's lump hammer, and every part of the right picture except for the tiny tie-detail area. Input 2 is a close-up of the two flaws in the right image, not a request to crop the output.

The existing rope's height, weathered pale blue-grey three-strand texture, two short old ends, and one crossed figure-of-eight wrap are correct and should stay recognisable. The relative positions of the wooden post and real green stem stay exactly as they are. On the visible front of the stalk, bring the near arc of the rope into visible, gentle contact with a small clear area of green stalk (a continuous shadow at the point of contact and a slight flattening of the old rope's inner edge). If necessary nudge an immediately adjacent small sprout or leaf stem behind the rope locally, while keeping the neighbouring buds. The near arc lies over the intact stalk, the far arc clearly goes BEHIND the stalk, with a little ease behind for growth. Never bury the rope under green tissue, catch a leaf stalk, or leave a halo there. Keep a single crossover between the plant and stake.

Crucially, REMOVE the full upside-down U-shaped handle currently hovering over the rope. Replace it with a properly driven small metal fencing staple, on the front face of the stake at exactly the same high tie. The two pointed legs are buried straight INTO THE FRONT FACE OF THE WOOD, pointing away from the camera. You cannot see the shape of the two metal legs, their tips are hidden inside the wood. Only the short grey rounded crown is visible, along with its two contact points disappearing into tiny dimples in the timber: ONE point ABOVE the rope, ONE point BELOW the rope. The visible crown looks like one short, almost vertical dull galvanised metal bar with a slight diagonal slant, straddling ONE run of the rope like a miniature close-fitting bridge. The crown touches and very slightly compresses the rope and follows its round profile, with a small realistic dark contact shadow; fits closely over the material. It does not look like an upside-down silver U viewed front on, a paper clip, a large handle, or two exposed dangling legs. It is a real small roughly 15 mm fitted staple, approximately a third of the width of the squared timber. Keep the loop neatly secured near the top and preserve the rope around the timber. Show its shadows in the actual daylight and grain of the original.

This is a small repair on a finished printed instructional image. Keep the plant canopy, every other leaf and colour, the left image, small sprout buds, ground, hands, tool and matching allotment view as close as possible to the full-resolution input. No text, inset, labels, borders or zoomed panel.
